strengths: Strong and highly intuitive motivation: Shifting from same-programmer iterative edits (which often suffer from 'cognitive inertia') to cross-programmer solutions allows the model to learn global algorithmic shifts rather than local micro-optimizations.

Rigorous evaluation setup: The use of the gem5 CPU simulator ensures deterministic execution time measurements, avoiding the noise of real hardware. Compiling with -O3 ensures that the measured performance gains represent high-level algorithmic innovations rather than optimizations that compilers can automatically perform.

Insightful diagnosis of the correctness vs. performance trade-off: The paper correctly identifies that training on aggressive problem-oriented pairs significantly improves speedup but reduces compilation and functional correctness. It offers a solid analysis of why this occurs.

Simple and highly effective mitigation: Using weight-space model merging (Linear and Slerp) to combine a conservative model (trained on user-oriented pairs) with an aggressive model (trained on problem-oriented pairs) is a clever and highly successful way to balance correctness and optimization magnitude.
Substantial empirical improvements: The proposed approach leads to outstanding gains, boosting the optimization ratio to 76.65% and the speedup factor to 5.09x on the DeepSeek-Coder 33B model.
weaknesses: Lack of cross-ablation on instruction style: For PIE-User, the authors used performance-conditioned tagging, while for PIE-Problem, they used simple instructions. It would be more systematic to evaluate both datasets under both instruction formats to untangle the effect of the prompting template from the training data.

Limited technical novelty in the model merging method itself: The paper relies on existing off-the-shelf model merging techniques (Linear, Slerp) without introducing new alignment or merging mechanisms custom-tailored for code semantics.

Evaluation is restricted to a single language (C++): While C++ is the standard performance-oriented language and inherits the setup from the original PIE dataset, demonstrating similar trends in languages like Python or Java would further strengthen the generalizability of the findings.

strengths: Novel and Insightful Core Concept: The critique of the previous PIE dataset (which focuses on iterative edits from the same programmer) as being limited to local/conservative optimizations is highly intuitive. Proposing a 'problem-oriented' perspective to force the model to learn global/algorithmic optimizations from different programmers is a strong contribution.

Deterministic and Rigorous Evaluation System: Evaluating the speedup on top of GCC -O3 compiler optimization using the gem5 CPU simulator is excellent. It ensures the reported speedup is real (not just trivial things a compiler already does) and deterministic (avoiding hardware/OS scheduling noise).

Effective Solution to the Correctness-Optimization Tradeoff: Shifting to aggressive algorithmic optimization naturally degrades code correctness. The authors creatively address this bottleneck by using model merging (Linear and Slerp) to combine the 'conservative' user-oriented model with the 'aggressive' problem-oriented model. This represents a highly practical and novel application of LLM merging.
Convincing Empirical Performance: The experimental results show substantial gains. For DeepSeek-Coder 33B, %OPT increases from 51.76% to 76.65% and Speedup increases from 2.65x to 5.09x under Best@8.

Clear and Informative Code Case Studies: The manuscript provides excellent, readable C++ code examples (e.g., Figures 2, 8, 9, 10) which clearly demonstrate the shift from local constant-factor optimization (e.g., fast I/O) to global time-complexity optimization (e.g., from O(N^2) to O(1) query time).
weaknesses: Decline in Best@1 Correctness: Under PIE-Problem, the correctness of the code drops dramatically at Best@1 (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder 33B drops from 59.49% to 37.41%). Although model merging improves this to 48.03%, it is still notably lower than the PIE-User baseline (59.49%). For practical software engineering tools, maintaining a high correctness rate at low k is critical. The authors should discuss how this degradation might be further mitigated.

Analysis of the 90% Improvement Threshold: The PIE-Problem dataset is filtered using a strict relative improvement threshold of 90%. While this targets order-of-magnitude algorithmic changes, it would be highly informative to see an ablation study or discussion on how varying this threshold (e.g., 50% or 75%) impacts the dataset size, model performance, and optimization quality.

Details of LoRA Merging: The training section mentions that the models are fine-tuned using LoRA. However, the details on how model merging was performed on LoRA adapters are somewhat sparse. Clarifying whether the authors merged the LoRA weights directly, or folded them back into the base models before merging, would improve reproducibility.

Dataset Scale and Diversity: As shown in Table 1, the unique problems in PIE-Problem Train (336) are much fewer than in PIE-User Train (1,135). The paper would benefit from a brief discussion on the feasibility of scaling the problem-oriented approach to more diverse or real-world software domains beyond competitive programming.

strengths: Clear Motivation and Intuitive Concept: Shifting from a user-oriented perspective (iterative edits by the same programmer, which often suffer from cognitive inertia and local refactoring) to a problem-oriented perspective (edits across different programmers) is a well-justified and highly effective paradigm shift for high-level code optimization.

Solid Empirical Results: The proposed PIE-Problem dataset enables fine-tuned models to achieve massive gains in both the optimization ratio (%OPT) and speedup (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder 33B going from 51.76% to 71.03% %OPT and 2.649x to 4.812x speedup). This is particularly impressive given that the PIE-Problem training dataset is 4x smaller than the original PIE-User.

Innovative Solution to Correctness Trade-off: The paper identifies a clear trade-off: problem-oriented training leads to high speedup but lower correctness, while user-oriented training is conservative (high correctness but low speedup). Proposing to merge these two models using weight-merging techniques (Merge-Linear and Slerp) to achieve the best of both worlds is an elegant, simple, and highly effective solution.

Rigorous Evaluation Setup: The authors use GCC -O3 compilation and the gem5 CPU simulator to measure running times deterministically. This ensures that the measured performance improvements are genuine and not artifacts of system noise or basic compiler-level optimizations.
weaknesses: Scope and Real-World Generalizability: The dataset is restricted to C++ competitive programming problems (from CodeNet/PIE). While competitive programming is excellent for evaluating algorithmic optimization, it represents a narrow domain. High-level optimizations in real-world software engineering often involve API usage, database queries, memory management, or architectural changes, which are not captured here.

Lack of Qualitative Analysis on Merged Models: While the quantitative benefits of model merging are clear, the paper lacks a qualitative analysis of what the merged model actually generates. Does it selectively choose between local and global optimizations depending on the input, or does it generate a hybrid style of code?

Mathematical/Procedural Clarity in Dataset Construction: In Section 3, the definition of the trajectory $Y_x^p$ and the pairing set $P_p$ is slightly hand-wavy (e.g., "$P_p = \{(y_1^{u_1}, y_1^{u_2}), (y_1^{u_1}, y_1^{u_3}), \dots\}$" is listed without a general rule). A precise mathematical definition of which pairs from the sorted list are selected (beyond the 90% threshold) would improve clarity and reproducibility.

strengths: The transition from a 'user-oriented' to a 'problem-oriented' perspective for code optimization pair construction is an intuitive, elegant, and highly effective idea that addresses a key limitation of existing datasets (i.e., the cognitive inertia of a single programmer).

The multi-dimensional analysis (structural via Control Flow Graphs, semantic via embeddings, and categorization via human/LLM analysis) is exceptionally thorough and clearly demonstrates the qualitative differences between the two pair-construction paradigms.

The proposed 'Anchor Verification' framework is a clever and highly practical way to address the 'optimization tax' (correctness trade-off) by exploiting the unique property of the code optimization task: the availability of a slow but functionally correct reference program to act as an execution oracle.

The evaluation is extensive, demonstrating substantial performance improvements across multiple advanced models (including Qwen2.5-Coder, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3) across several metrics (%OPT, SPEEDUP, CORRECT).
weaknesses: Details on PCO pair selection and construction could be clearer. Although Section 3.2 mentions selecting the same number of pairs per problem as PIE based on top speedup rankings, it is not fully clear if this selection introduces a bias or if the 'slow' programs in some pairs are already highly optimized, which might reduce their training value.

The evaluation is restricted to competitive programming (CP) problems from CodeNet. CP tasks heavily emphasize algorithmic shifts, whereas real-world software engineering code optimization often involves different paradigms such as database query optimization, memory allocation, API choices, or caching.

There is a lack of cost and efficiency analysis for the Anchor Verification mechanism. Running a 3-stage framework with test-case generation, execution, and iterative refinement can be computationally expensive and time-consuming; a breakdown of the trade-off between execution wall-clock time, token costs, and performance improvement would enhance the paper.

strengths: The conceptual shift from a user-oriented perspective (sequential iteration of a single programmer) to a problem-oriented perspective (comparing different programmers' solutions) is a highly intuitive and effective way to construct code optimization datasets, allowing LLMs to learn global algorithmic optimizations rather than just incremental changes.

The proposed 'Anchor Verification' framework is elegantly simple yet practically powerful. It successfully capitalizes on the unique property of code optimization where the 'slow code' serves as a reliable functional oracle to generate and verify test cases, effectively mitigating the functional correctness 'optimization tax'.

The paper presents a comprehensive and rigorous evaluation utilizing state-of-the-art LLMs (including Qwen2.5-Coder, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3), demonstrating substantial and consistent improvements in optimization ratio, correctness, and speedup.

Excellent qualitative and quantitative analyses are provided, including Graph Edit Distance (GED) on control flow graphs, semantic t-SNE visualizations, human/LLM-based categorization of optimization types, and data-efficiency studies.
weaknesses: The scalability of the Problem-Oriented Code Optimization (PCO) data generation method might be limited in real-world software development. Unlike competitive programming platforms (e.g., CodeNet), real-world repository development rarely yields dozens of diverse, functionally equivalent implementations of the same complex function from different programmers to construct such training pairs.

Selecting PCO pairs based strictly on the 'top speedup rankings' to control for dataset size when comparing to PIE might bias the dataset towards extremely large algorithmic jumps. The authors should discuss how this selection bias affects the model's ability to learn more nuanced or moderate optimization patterns.
Minor mathematical notation clarity issues exist, such as the formulation of the dataset scaling equations in Section 3.1, which could be explained with more explicit definitions of the variables.

strengths: Novel and Intuitive Dataset Perspective: Shifting from a user-oriented (incremental, single-programmer) to a problem-oriented (cross-programmer, speed-sorted) perspective is an elegant and highly effective approach to constructing code optimization datasets. It allows LLMs to learn global, algorithmic improvements rather than just local micro-optimizations.

Thorough Multi-Dimensional Analysis: The paper provides a comprehensive analysis (CFG Edit Distance, semantic embedding visualization via t-SNE, and human/LLM categorization) demonstrating that the new PCO dataset contains significantly more global/algorithmic modifications than the PIE baseline.

Practical & Logical Verification Mechanism: The 'Anchor Verification' method is a clever application of differential testing. By using the slow but functionally correct program as a test oracle, the framework solves a key challenge in LLM code optimization (correctness regression/optimization tax) without relying on external oracle test suites.

Strong Empirical Results: Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art models (including Qwen2.5-Coder 32B, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3) demonstrate significant improvements in both speedup and functional correctness.
weaknesses: Mathematical Error in Scaling Formulas: In Section 3.1 (Page 4), the formulas for the scaling of optimization pairs contain a redundant 1/2 multiplier. The combination symbol $C_n^2$ already denotes the number of unordered pairs of size 2. Since the submissions are sorted by runtime, each pair has a unique directed path (from slower to faster), meaning the number of valid pairs is exactly $C_n^2$. Multiplying by 1/2 again is mathematically incorrect and halves the actual number of pairs.

Limited Discussion on Differential Testing Literature: The concept of using a correct-but-slow program as an oracle to test and verify a fast-but-potentially-incorrect program is fundamentally equivalent to differential testing or equivalence testing, which has a long history in Software Engineering. The paper should position 'Anchor Verification' more clearly within this context and discuss related SE literature.

Heuristic Test Case Coverage: In Stage 1 of Anchor Verification, the LLM generates only 3 test inputs. While this improves correctness, competitive programming problems usually require dozens of edge-case tests. The paper does not thoroughly explore how the number of generated test inputs affects the correctness rate vs. computational overhead during verification.

Minor Formatting and Layout Issues: Some tables (e.g., Table 4) are referenced in the main text on page 8 but actually placed on page 14 without optimal layout alignment, which slightly disrupts the reading flow.

strengths: Proposes a highly intuitive yet powerful paradigm shift from a user-oriented perspective (incremental local edits) to a problem-oriented perspective (global algorithmic modifications) for constructing code optimization pairs.

Effectively addresses the data scarcity bottleneck in code optimization datasets, showing mathematically and empirically how aggregating across multiple users increases training data volume and diversity.

Introduces a clever 'Anchor Verification Framework' that uses the unoptimized but functionally correct 'slow code' as an oracle to evaluate test inputs generated by LLMs, overcoming the correctness trade-off ('optimization tax') without relying on buggy synthetic test outputs.

Provides a remarkably comprehensive evaluation: testing across multiple state-of-the-art models (Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o), verifying results on a cycle-accurate simulator (gem5) as well as physical hardware (Intel Xeon CPUs), and demonstrating cross-language generalization (C++ and Python).

Conducts meticulous and insightful ablation studies, including a structural analysis via Graph Edit Distance (GED), a comparison to isolate selection bias versus perspective shift, and an evaluation of multi-iteration refinement.
weaknesses: The 'Anchor Verification' assumes the original 'slow code' can execute within a reasonable timeframe. If the slow code encounters Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) or infinite loops for certain edge-case inputs generated by the LLM, the verification step could hang or become extremely costly. Although the authors briefly discuss mitigation strategies in Appendix L, a deeper analysis of such failure modes in the main text would be valuable.
The paper features some minor typographical errors, such as 'anchor verifiaction' (page 3), 'Comparion Group' (page 9), and 'REMAING' (page 17).

strengths: Innovative Perspective Shift: Shifting the dataset construction paradigm from user-oriented trajectories (which are constrained by a single programmer's thought process) to problem-oriented trajectories is a simple, elegant, and highly effective idea. This enables Code LLMs to learn global algorithmic improvements (such as moving from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$) rather than mere local syntax cleanups.

Well-designed Anchor Verification Framework: The proposed framework cleverly exploits the unique property of the code optimization task—that the starting 'slow code' is functionally correct. Using it as a trusted gold-standard anchor to execute generated inputs and obtain verified test cases elegantly solves the 'optimization tax' (correctness loss) without relying on potentially buggy synthetic test case outputs.

Thorough Multi-dimensional Analysis: The paper provides excellent analytical support for its claims, including structural analysis using Graph Edit Distance (GED), semantic clustering using t-SNE, human and LLM classification of optimization types, and detailed failure mode studies.

Comprehensive Evaluation: Experiments are conducted over multiple state-of-the-art models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen2.5-Coder) across two languages (C++ and Python). The authors also include vital practical validations, such as execution on physical hardware and detailed latency overhead breakdowns.
weaknesses: Assumption of Uniform Problem Definitions: The problem-oriented approach relies on having multiple solutions grouped under the exact same problem specifications (e.g., competitive programming platforms). In real-world software engineering contexts, grouping arbitrary pieces of code under a single 'problem' is more complex due to variations in requirements, external dependencies, and environmental contexts.

Potential Execution Bottleneck of Slow Code: During Stage 2 of Anchor Verification, test inputs are executed on the inefficient 'slow code'. If the original code has severe complexity issues (e.g., exponential time complexity), executing it on boundary inputs generated by the LLM might lead to severe timeouts. While the authors suggest mitigation strategies in Section L, a quantitative analysis of how frequently these timeouts occurred during their experiments would improve the paper.

Small Number of Test Cases: The framework generates only 3 test case inputs (as shown in Figure 12). It is unclear if 3 test cases are sufficient to ensure robust correctness for complex algorithmic tasks, and the paper lacks an ablation study evaluating performance and correctness across varying numbers of generated inputs.

strengths: Innovative Shift in Perspective: Proposing a problem-oriented perspective instead of a user-oriented one is a highly intuitive and effective way to overcome the cognitive limitations of a single developer, enabling LLMs to learn global algorithmic shifts rather than just local optimizations.

Rigorous Multi-Dimensional Dataset Analysis: The paper provides a thorough structural (using Graph Edit Distance on CFGs) and semantic (using embedding visualization) analysis showing that problem-oriented pairs exhibit substantially more diversity and complex algorithmic edits.

Practical and Sound Verification Method: The Anchor Verification Framework smartly exploits the unique property of the code optimization task—having a slow but functionally correct reference program. Utilizing it as an execution oracle to verify LLM-generated test inputs successfully bypasses the issue of LLM hallucination in generating complete test cases.

Strong Empirical Evaluation: The proposed approach is evaluated across a wide range of state-of-the-art models (Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3), shows consistent improvements on both C++ and Python, and is validated on physical hardware.
weaknesses: Missing Key Baseline (Synthesis from Problem Description): Since the problem-oriented perspective pairs completely different implementations from different developers, the model might just be learning to generate a new solution from scratch rather than truly 'optimizing' the input code. To prove that the 'slow code' is actually useful as a prompt, the authors should compare against a baseline that generates the fast code directly from the problem description without looking at the slow code.

Discrepancies in I/O and Format across Developers: Because different programmers might have different coding habits (e.g., using different fast I/O methods or minor format variations), pairing them can introduce format mismatches. This is supported by Table 7, where 31% of failures are due to 'input/output format failure'. This is a direct side-effect of the problem-oriented approach and limits its seamless application.

Limited Novelty in Anchor Verification: Using a reference implementation as an execution oracle to obtain ground-truth outputs for test case inputs is a well-established technique in differential testing and automated program repair. Its application to LLM code refinement is useful but represents an incremental novelty.

Evaluation of Test Suite Quality: The framework only generates 3 test case inputs (Appendix Q) for verification. Relying on such a small number of test cases might lead to overfitting (passing the 3 generated test cases but failing on the hidden test suite). A deeper analysis of test case coverage and its impact on the final correctness on the hidden test suite would strengthen the paper.
